title: Water in Water
summary: A great tree of the innate radiates through the three worlds, and in its sky-like nature no one is held in bonds; as water poured into water cannot be told apart, the mind-jewel enters the sky in the same taste, beyond self and other, birth and death, going and coming. Munidatta reads the tree as the innate mind of the lord of yogis, which pervades the three worlds (cp.43.m2), and calls the refrain an illustrative simile: the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta, and the lord of yogis become of same taste and enter clear light, where there is no apprehension of knowledge (cp.43.m3).

flags.note: The Bengali heading names only the rāga. The poet's name comes from the attribution bhūsukupādānāṃ ('of Bhūsukupāda'), which the manuscript writes before the song (the edition's emendation moves it out of 1a), and from the Tibetan heading, baM ga la zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called Baṅgāla, of Bhusukupāda'. Drop the name if headings should give only what the line itself has.

lines.gloss: innate · great tree · radiates · in the three worlds
lines.en: The [great tree]{mahataru} of the [innate]{sahaja} [radiates]{sphurana} through the [three worlds]{trailokya}.

flags.note: phariae is rendered 'radiates', the glossary's word (sphurana, 'radiate'). The Tibetan 'phro means both 'radiate' and 'spread', and for a tree 'spreads' may read more naturally; the glossary rendering is kept.
sahaja mahātaru can be 'the innate great tree' or 'the great tree of the innate'. The draft takes the second, as the Tibetan does with its genitive (lhan cig skyes pa'i shing chen).

lines.translit: khasamasabhābe re bāṇata kā koe || dhru ||
lines.gloss: in the sky-like nature · (particle) · in bonds · who · anyone (?) · (refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: bāṇata, apparently bāṇa with the locative -ta, is taken as 'in bonds' (glossary bandhana, 'bond', here in the plural), following the Tibetan bcings, 'bound', and Munidatta's paraphrase, where no one is bound or freed (cp.43.m2). bāṇa is also 'arrow' (compare the arrow of song 28), which would give 'who is in the arrow?'; that seems unlikely here.

kā koe is taken as 'who': kā is an interrogative, and koe may be 'anyone' or a verb ('is'?); the sense is not certain. The Tibetan line reads 'the nature equal to the sky: who, having been bound, is freed?' (nam mkha' dang mtshungs rang bzhin bcings nas grol ba gang), with a 'freed' the Bengali lacks; Munidatta's paraphrase also has 'bound or freed' (cp.43.m2).

Shastri prints ধ্রু, the cue to sing the refrain, already after this line, and again after couplets 2, 3 and 4; normally it follows the refrain and the later couplets only. Couplet 2 is kept as the refrain, as marked; see the note on couplet 2.

lines.translit: jima jale pāṇiā ṭaliā bheṛa na jāa
lines.gloss: as · in water · water · poured · difference · not · is known (or: goes)
lines.en: As [water in water]{water-in-water}, once poured, cannot be told apart,

flags.note: bheṛa na jāa is taken as 'the difference is not known', with Munidatta's na jñāyate (cp.43.m3), and rendered 'cannot be told apart'; na jāa could also be 'does not go'. The Tibetan line has 'cannot be separated' (dbye bar mi nus). ṭaliā, 'tipped, poured', is written ṭaliyā in the edition (য় is unstable); it might also mean 'shaken'. 'once poured' renders the participle.

lines.translit: tima maṇa raaṇā re samarase gaaṇa samāa || dhru ||
lines.gloss: so · mind (printed maraṇa, "death") · jewel (printed aaṇā) · (particle) · in same taste · sky · enters · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: so the [mind-jewel]{citta-ratna}, in the [same taste]{samarasa}, enters the [sky]{gagana}.

flags.note: Shastri prints maraṇa aaṇā, and the glossary tags maraṇa as 'death' (marana). Munidatta's paraphrase has 'the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta' (manobodhicittaratna, cp.43.m3), and the Tibetan line has yid kyi rin chen, 'jewel of the mind'. Both point to maṇa raaṇā, 'mind-jewel', with ṇa and ra transposed in the printed text; the draft adopts it. On the printed reading, aaṇā has no clear sense and the line does not construe well ('so death … in the same taste enters the sky').
'mind-jewel' uses the proposed entry citta-ratna; marana is listed in termsOmitted for this line. citta ('mind') and ratna ('jewel') could be marked separately instead.

lines.translit: jāsu ṇāhi appā tāsu parelā kāhi
lines.gloss: whose · is not · self · for him · others · where
lines.en: One who has no [self]{atman}: for him, where are others?

flags.note: Shastri prints jatpuṇāhi adhyātā svaparelā kāhi, which does not construe well. Munidatta cites the line as jāsuṇāhi and paraphrases: for the lord of yogis who has no relation of self and what is his own, the relation to others is remote (cp.43.m4). The Tibetan line has 'for whom there is no self, for him others …' (gang la gang la bdag nyid med pa de la gzhan dag). The draft reads jāsu ṇāhi appā tāsu parelā kāhi, taking jatpu-, adhyā- and sva- as misreadings of jāsu, appā and -su. Keeping Shastri's division, svaparelā would be 'self and other' (glossary sva-para): 'For one who has no self, where are self and other?'
kāhi is taken as 'where'; it may be 'what' ('what are others to him?'). parelā may be singular ('the other') or plural; the Tibetan gzhan dag is plural.

lines.translit: āi anuaṇā re jāmamaraṇabhaba ṇāhi || dhru ||
lines.gloss: from the beginning · unarisen · (particle) · birth-death-existence · is not · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: [Non-arising]{anutpada} from the beginning, there is no [birth]{janma}, [death]{marana} or [existence]{bhava}.

flags.note: jāmamaraṇabhaba is taken as three nouns, 'birth, death or existence', as in song 22; it could be 'the existence of birth and death', as the Tibetan has it (skye dang 'chi ba'i srid pa).

For āi anuaṇā, 'non-arising from the beginning', the Tibetan line has thog ma mtha' med, 'without beginning or end'. Shastri prints anuaṇāre as one word; re is taken as the particle that stands in each second half-line.

lines.translit: bhūsuku bhaṇai kaṭa rāutu bhaṇai kaṭa saalā eha sahāba
lines.gloss: Bhusuku · says · told · Rāutu · says · told · all · this · nature
lines.en: [Bhusuku]{p-bhusuku} says what was [told]{kata}, [Rāutu]{p-rautu} says what was [told]{kata}: this is the [nature]{svabhava} of all.

flags.note: kaṭa (twice) is rendered 'told' after Munidatta, who explains it as 'the meaning stated before' (cp.43.m5): Bhusuku and Rāutu restate what was said. The Tibetan line has ngo mtshar, 'wonder', as for akaṭa elsewhere (glossary adbhuta); where Munidatta has 'stated before', the Tibetan comment has 'said directly' (mngon sum du gsungs pa), and the word could also come from prakaṭa, 'plain, manifest' (compare prakaṭayati in cp.43.m1). Alternatives: 'Bhusuku says: a wonder!' or 'Bhusuku says plainly'.

Rāutu speaks beside Bhusuku again, as in song 41, and is kept as a name (glossary p-rautu). Here the Tibetan has rjes smras, 'said afterwards, then said', not a name, and Munidatta passes over him, saying only that Bhusukupāda speaks (cp.43.m5).

saalā eha sahāba is rendered 'this is the nature of all', after Munidatta's 'this is the true nature of all things' (cp.43.m5); it could also be 'all this is (its) nature'. The Tibetan line ends ngo mtshar kun, 'all a wonder', with no word for nature.

lines.translit: jāi ṇa ābai re ṇa taṃhi bhābābhāba || dhru ||
lines.gloss: goes · not · comes · (particle) · not · there · being and nonbeing · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: It does not go or come; there is no [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava} there.

flags.note: jāi ṇa ābai, with one ṇa between the two verbs, is taken as 'does not go or come', as the Tibetan ('gro 'ong dang bral, 'free of going and coming') and Munidatta (no coming and going is seen, cp.43.m5) read it. If ṇa negates only ābai, the line says 'it goes and does not come back'. The edition's ābayi is written ābai (য় is unstable).

notes.text: Munidatta opens by saying that Bhusukupāda, delighted by the intoxication of the innate (sahajamadamudita), makes that same meaning plain (cp.43.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has him 'satisfied with the bliss of the innate' (lhan cig skyes pa'i bde bas tshim pa) and calls him 'du shes gsum pa'i zhabs, its name for Bhusuku. For 'that same meaning' it has de kho na nyid kyi don, usually 'the meaning of reality', perhaps a literal rendering of tam eva, 'that very'.

re, which stands in the middle of each second half-line (1b, 2b, 4b; in 3b Shastri prints it joined to the word before, anuaṇāre), is an exclamatory particle ('O', 'ah') that fills out the line. It is left untranslated, as is ধ্রু, the cue to sing the refrain.

Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung. Baṅgāla, also a name of Bengal, is the rāga of this song; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes it (baM ga la) and names the poet (b+hu su ku'i zhabs).

The song opens with a single great tree whose spread reaches through the three worlds (the realms of desire, form and the formless; here, the whole world). Nothing more is said of the tree; the next line turns to a nature like the sky. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees: lhan cig skyes pa'i shing chen 'jig rten gsum na 'phro, 'the great tree of the innate radiates in the three worlds'.

Munidatta's paraphrase puts the innate mind (sahajacitta) of the lord of yogis where the song has the great tree: through contact with the dust of the guru's feet it has taken the seed that has the form of the bliss of the union of vajra and lotus, and it radiates, pervading the three worlds. Through its sky-like nature of bliss no one in the three worlds is bound or freed (so the Tibetan; on the Sanskrit see the witness note on 1b); he adds bliss where the song has only the sky-like nature. He supports this with the Dvikalpa (the Hevajra): the world is pervaded by bliss, in the form of pervaded and pervader (cp.43.m2). The Tibetan comment agrees, calling the sky-like 'the example equal to the sky' (nam mkha' dang mtshungs pa'i dpe) and the nature 'the nature of great bliss'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nam mkha' dang mtshungs rang bzhin bcings nas grol ba gang, 'the nature equal to the sky: who, having been bound, is freed?', with a 'freed' the Bengali lacks; its bcings, 'bound', supports taking bāṇata as 'in bonds'. Munidatta's Sanskrit, na ko vidvān mukto vā, 'no one learned (?) or freed', wants a word for 'bound' where it has vidvān; the Tibetan comment has bcings pa dang grol ba med pa, 'neither bound nor freed' (cp.43.m2).

bāṇata looks like bāṇa with the locative -ta, 'in bāṇa'; the glossary files it under bond (bandhana), as if bāṇa stood for bandha, 'binding'. The same word means 'arrow' (compare the arrow of song 28). In kā koe, kā is an interrogative, 'who'; koe may be 'anyone', or a verb.

Couplet 2 is kept as the refrain, as marked, but Munidatta's count sits awkwardly with that. He usually leaves the refrain out when he numbers the verses; here he introduces couplet 2 as his 'second verse' (dvitīyapadena, cp.43.m3), couplet 3 as his 'third' (cp.43.m4) and couplet 4 as his 'fourth' (cp.43.m5), and his comment on couplet 2 does not call it the refrain. At the end of his comment on couplet 1 he says 'by the verse that follows the verse, the refrain is to be understood' (padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyaṃ; the Tibetan comment has tshig phyi ma'i rkang pas d+h+rU'i rkang par rig par bya'o, cp.43.m2). That can be read as naming the following couplet the refrain, or as saying that the refrain, couplet 1, is to be sung after each following verse; Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b would fit the second reading.

Water poured into water: once it is in, the poured water cannot be told from the water it joins. The refrain makes this the first half of an 'as … so' comparison (jima … tima). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has water 'placed' in water, which 'cannot be separated' (dper na chu la chu bzhag dbye bar mi nus ltar).

Munidatta calls the refrain an illustrative simile (dṛṣṭāntopamā): as the wise do not know the difference of outer water falling into other water, so the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta, and the lord of yogis become of same taste and enter the sky, which he explains as entering clear light; there, there is no apprehension of knowledge. He quotes a scripture: as water placed in water, so the wheel of knowledge abides (cp.43.m3). Where the Sanskrit says the wise do not know the difference, the Tibetan comment says the intelligent know the waters as undivided (dbyer med par blo dang ldan pas shes so).

Shastri prints maraṇa aaṇā. Munidatta's paraphrase (manobodhicittaratna, 'the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta', cp.43.m3) and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), whose line has yid kyi rin chen, 'jewel of the mind', and whose comment has yid nyid byang chub kyi sems rin po che, both point to maṇa raaṇā, 'mind-jewel'; the printed text looks like a transposition of ṇa and ra. The draft follows that reading and does not use the glossary's 'death' (marana) here.

The printed line, jatpuṇāhi adhyātā svaparelā kāhi, is read as jāsu ṇāhi appā tāsu parelā kāhi, 'one who has no self, for him where are others?'. Munidatta's citation of the line (jāsuṇāhītyādi) and his paraphrase, 'for whom … there is no relation of self and what is his own, for him the relation to others …' (yasya … tasya parasambandhaḥ, cp.43.m4), support jāsu … tāsu, 'whose … for him'. So does the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): gang la gang la bdag nyid med pa de la gzhan dag dang, 'for whom there is no self, for him others and …', which runs on into 3b.

Munidatta introduces couplet 3, his 'third verse', as stating the true nature of things (bhāvasvarūpa). For the lord of yogis who has no relation of self and what is his own, the relation to others is remote (the Sanskrit itaratara is unclear; the Tibetan has 'very distant', shin tu ring du). Since things are unarisen, accomplished persons (siddhapuruṣa) do not see their arising, abiding and perishing. He quotes a scripture: not born and not dead, not with form nor beyond form, neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, it is indicated by the letter na (cp.43.m4); for the last phrase the Tibetan has 'free of action, it is indicated by that' (byed pa dang bral de yis mtshon).

For āi anuaṇā, 'non-arising from the beginning', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has thog ma mtha' med, 'without beginning or end', and it takes the compound as 'the existence of birth and death': thog ma mtha' med skye dang 'chi ba'i srid pa med.

kaṭa: Munidatta explains it as 'the meaning stated before' (kaṭam iti pūrvoktārthaṃ, cp.43.m5), so 'told', perhaps from a form of kathita. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders it ngo mtshar, 'wonder', as akaṭa is read elsewhere (glossary adbhuta), and its comment glosses that word as what Bhusukupāda 'said directly' (mngon sum du gsungs pa) where the Sanskrit has 'stated before'. A link with prakaṭa, 'plain, manifest', is also possible; Munidatta's opening says Bhusukupāda makes the meaning plain (prakaṭayati, cp.43.m1).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads b+hu su kus smras ngo mtshar rjes smras ngo mtshar kun, 'Bhusuku said: a wonder; then (he) said: a wonder; all …', with rjes smras, 'then said', where the Bengali names Rāutu. Munidatta passes over Rāutu and says only that Bhusukupāda speaks (cp.43.m5). As in song 41, whether Rāutu (Old Bengali rāuta, 'prince') is a second speaker or a title of Bhusuku is uncertain.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4, his 'fourth verse', as again stating the true nature of things. kaṭa is the meaning stated before; Bhusukupāda says that this is the true nature of all things: here, through profound innate joy and by giving up concepts of being and nonbeing, no yogin is seen coming and going in the prison of saṃsāra (jinasaṃsārakārāgāre, unclear; the Tibetan has 'birth in saṃsāra, entering the house of conduct, or coming', as if reading janma for jina and cāra for kāra). He ends with an Apabhraṃśa dohā of Saraha, which the Tibetan renders: profundity itself cannot be indicated; it is not apprehended as self or other; the fruit of innate joy is known by self-awareness itself (cp.43.m5).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'gro 'ong dang bral de la dngos dang dngos med med, 'free of going and coming, there is no being and nonbeing there', which supports taking ṇa with both verbs. Munidatta's comment likewise speaks of no coming and going (yātāyāta) being seen (cp.43.m5).

termsOmitted.reason: Shastri prints maraṇa ('death'), but Munidatta's manobodhicittaratna (cp.43.m3) and the Tibetan yid kyi rin chen point to maṇa raaṇā, 'mind-jewel', which the draft adopts (proposal citta-ratna); flagged for the reviewer.
Tibetan rin chen only; 'jewel' is rendered inside the proposed term citta-ratna ('mind-jewel').

The draft reads svaparelā as (tā)su parelā, 'for him … others', following Munidatta's tasya parasambandhaḥ (cp.43.m4) and the Tibetan de la gzhan dag; on Shastri's division it would be 'self and other' (given as the alternative in the flag).
Tibetan ngo mtshar only; the Bengali kaṭa is rendered 'told' after Munidatta (proposal kata), with 'wonder' given as an alternative in the flag.
Tibetan 'gro 'ong only; the Bengali has two verbs, jāi ṇa ābai, rendered 'does not go or come'.

forms.translit: yid nyid byang chub kyi sems rin po che

proposals.definition: The mind pictured as a jewel. In the refrain of song 43 (2b), where Shastri prints maraṇa aaṇā, Munidatta's paraphrase (manobodhicittaratna) and the Tibetan line (yid kyi rin chen) point to maṇa raaṇa, 'mind-jewel', which enters the sky in the same taste. Compare king of mind, which Munidatta also calls the jewel of mind.
proposals.symbolicImage: a jewel that is the mind

symbolicReadings.referent: the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta (manobodhicittaratna), which with the lord of yogis becomes of same taste and enters clear light, where there is no apprehension of knowledge; his paraphrase of the refrain, not an explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment agrees (yid nyid byang chub kyi sems rin po che)

proposals.rationale: 2b is drafted on the reading maṇa raaṇa, which Munidatta and the Tibetan support. An entry gives the phrase one rendering and keeps the printed maraṇa ('death') from being tagged as death in this line. If the reviewer prefers, citta ('mind') and ratna ('jewel') can be marked separately instead.

proposals.definition: Old Bengali kaṭa, which follows 'says' twice in Bhusuku's signature line (song 43, 4a). Munidatta explains it as 'the meaning stated before', hence 'told'. The Tibetan line has ngo mtshar, 'wonder', as for akaṭa elsewhere (see wonder), and its comment speaks of what was said directly; a link with prakaṭa, 'manifest', is possible.
proposals.rationale: A hard word the glossary lacks. An entry records the draft's choice ('told', after Munidatta, cp.43.m5) and the two alternatives, for the reviewer and for later songs.

questions: Refrain: couplet 2 is kept as the refrain, as marked. But Munidatta counts it as his 'second verse' (cp.43.m3), with couplets 3 and 4 as his 'third' and 'fourth' (cp.43.m4, cp.43.m5); Shastri prints ধ্রু already after 1b; and Munidatta's padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyaṃ (cp.43.m2) can be read as making couplet 1 the refrain, to be sung after each later verse. Should the marking stay on couplet 2, and should this song be noted as an exception to the brief's rule that Munidatta leaves the refrain out of his count?

2b: do you accept maṇa raaṇā, 'mind-jewel' (Munidatta's manobodhicittaratna, the Tibetan yid kyi rin chen), over the printed maraṇa aaṇā, which the glossary tags as 'death'? If so, should the proposed entry citta-ratna ('mind-jewel') stand, or would you rather mark citta and ratna separately?

3a: is the reading jāsu ṇāhi appā tāsu parelā kāhi ('One who has no self: for him, where are others?'), supported by Munidatta's lemma and paraphrase and by the Tibetan, acceptable? Or should the draft keep Shastri's division and render svaparelā as 'self and other' (glossary sva-para)?

4a: kaṭa is rendered 'told' (Munidatta: 'the meaning stated before'). The Tibetan has 'wonder', and 'plainly' (from prakaṭa) is also possible. Which do you want, and should the proposed entry kata stand?
4a: Rāutu is kept as a second speaker, as in song 41, although the Tibetan has rjes smras ('then said') and Munidatta ignores him. Confirm, or treat Rāutu as a title of Bhusuku?
1b: bāṇata is rendered 'in bonds' (glossary bandhana, 'bond', in the plural). Is the plural surface acceptable, or should 'bound' be added as a variant of the entry?
1a: the glossary's 'radiate' for phariae gives 'the great tree … radiates'. Would 'spreads', also a sense of the Tibetan 'phro, be better for a tree, perhaps as a variant of sphurana?
4b: 'It does not go or come' (with the Tibetan and Munidatta), or 'It goes and does not come back' (ṇa negating only ābai)?
h1: the heading adds 'Bhusukupāda' from the attribution written before the song and from the Tibetan heading, following the brief's heading pattern. Keep it?

2a: 'water in water' is kept in the glossary's wording ('As water in water, once poured, cannot be told apart'). Is 'once poured' acceptable for the participle ṭaliā, or would you prefer the freer 'As water poured into water'?
